items.content:
Most “authentic” posts on LinkedIn are completely useless.
There’s an easy fix to make sure yours aren’t.

If your personal posts are falling flat, it's likely because they're giving nothing.

Personal stories are a great tool for your personal brand - they can build trust quickly.

They show people what shaped you, how you think, and what you have learned along the way.

But the story still needs to give the reader a lesson, a takeaway, or a change they can make today. 

Here’s how to do it without being cringe:

1/ Start with the moment

Choose one specific event, conversation, or result that changed how you think. Give people the details they need to understand it, but cut anything that does not move the story forward.

Earlier this year, I met with a founder who runs a recruiting business for AI startups. Eight years in, his business is doing $65M a year, completely bootstrapped.

I was telling him how I'm the bottleneck in my business, because I can't find anyone as good at creating content as me.

He was polite, but said one thing that made me rethink everything: "You've got an imaginary scarcity mindset.” 

2/ Name the lesson

Explain what the experience taught you. The best lesson is usually something you now do differently because of what happened.

In my case, the lesson was simple. The talent wasn't missing...my willingness to actually go look for it was.

3/ Make it useful

Be clear with your readers how they can apply the lesson to their own work or life. Give them a question to ask themselves, common mistakes to avoid, or one action they can take.

To avoid imaginary scarcity, find someone a few years ahead of you. Tell them what you think is holding you back, and let them tell you which parts are real and which parts you made up.

An authentic, personal story earns the reader's attention when it teaches them something they can use.

I talked through this exact problem and more with Lakshmi Rebecca on her podcast. Check out the full episode here: https://lnkd.in/d_qP3AnQ

7 Japanese Concepts That Will Change How You Work:

Most people feel like they're drowning in work.

But some people stay calm through chaos.

Sometimes the best answers come from ancient wisdom.
And these timeless principles still work today.

Here are 7 Japanese conacepts you need to know:

1/ Wabi-Sabi: Embrace Imperfection

↳ Chase progress not perfection - ship at 70%.
↳ Share a work-in-progress update, not just polished results. Show the messy middle.

2/ Shoshin: Beginner's Mind

↳ Ask the dumb questions in meetings
↳ Say "I don't know but I'll find out" more

3/ Shokunin: Master Your Craft

↳ Pick the top up and coming skill you need in your industry. Block 30 minutes daily.
↳ DM someone great at it. Ask one question. Learn from real experience.

4/ Kaizen: Get 1% Better Everyday

↳ Every evening, write one tiny thing you'll do better tomorrow.
↳ End projects with: What worked? What didn't? What's next?

5/ Shikata ga nai: Accepting the Unchangeable

↳ Sort concerns: "My control" vs. "Not my control." Act accordingly.
↳ Use the 10-minute rule. Address it briefly, then decide.

6/ Kintsugi: Your Failures Are Your Best Stories

↳ Name three lessons from each setback. Write them down.
↳ Share lessons learned. Prevent repeat mistakes.

7/ Ikigai: Finding Your Purpose

↳ Track what energizes you. Reorganize your calendar around it.
↳ Map skills to market needs. Improve your market value.

I've seen hundreds transform their work with these principles.

I applied Shoshin when I started posting on LinkedIn 2 years ago.

No sales? Slow growth? Low trust?

Growing but nobody comments? Try Trust posts.

Posting daily and stuck at 2k followers? Double down on Grow posts.

A Trust post gives someone the opportunity to actually care about YOU, not just your ideas.

This is where you show your process, your behind-the-scenes, the messy parts most people leave out. "My wife quit her $250,000 job to work with me" works because it's specific and real.

3/ Sell Posts

Sell posts are the closers. Once someone recognizes you and trusts you, it’s time to give them a reason to buy from you.

Think transformational client stories, before and after case studies, breaking down a process and showing how it works to create value.

Before you write your next post, ask yourself where your LinkedIn is falling short.

Then choose 1 of these 3 posts as the fix.

items.content:
It is STILL possible to grow on LinkedIn in 2026.
 If I was starting again, this is the system I’d use:

Most people skip straight to the writing. They open a blank page and try to think of something extremely profound.

But if you want to grow, most of the work needs to be done before you open that blank page.

Here's what to do:

1/ Write 3 different types of posts

Every post has one job. Growth posts reach new people through broad topics. Trust posts show how a person actually thinks and works. Sales posts use proof to give people a reason to buy.

Growth posts have the best shot at going viral, but the other two are what make the audience worth having.

2/ Identify your niche and stick to it

Pick a niche with valuable lessons to teach, then stay in that lane. Career development is a broad one that consistently does well.

Random, trend-driven posts might get a spike, but they attract followers who never come back.

3/ Create a content funnel

The mix matters as much as the posts. Aim for 4 growth posts, 2 trust posts, and 1 sales post each week.

Growth gets broader reach but rarely sticks. Trust makes a creator feel like a real person. Sales targets the followers who are already ready to buy.

4/ Choose proven post topics

There's no need to invent formats from scratch. Pick a trending topic or format in each category and adapt it to the niche.

Newsjacking, educational posts, objection posts and case studies are all easy to do on any topic.

5/ Nail every hook

The first 2 lines decide whether anyone reads the rest. I use 9 hook types, and the most reliable ones lead with real numbers, challenge what everyone believes, or say one thing whilst implying another.

I spend at LEAST half the writing time on the hook alone.

6/ Make your posts readable

Write the same way people speak, because no one wants to read an academic paper on LinkedIn. Follow a set structure based on the goal of your post. 

Avoid AI slop - people want to read YOUR thoughts, not Claude’s.

7/ Prioritize quality visuals

Any visual - infographic, carousel, video, selfie - can go viral. What matters most is that it’s high quality, striking enough to stop the scroll, and related to the content you’re posting about.

Growth on LinkedIn looks like luck from the outside.

In reality, it's seven decisions made before you press post.

I paid $1500 to learn how to build a personal brand.
This is everything I learned:

When most people start posting, they focus on the complete wrong thing.
They tweak the headline, switch niches, try a new format every week, write like they’re sending a formal memo and wonder why nothing sticks.

It makes posting really hard. But they just never got handed the rules, so they guess, and guessing does not compound.

Doing it right comes down to 19 laws:

1/ Solve one clear problem

Choose one problem your audience actually cares about and keep coming back to it.

2/ Treat your profile like a landing page

Show what you do in five seconds or people bounce.

3/ Give your headline one job

Spell out who you help, what you help with, and one piece of proof.

4/ Write longer posts

Give the idea room instead of squeezing it into a caption.

5/ Write like you speak

Read every post out loud and cut anything that sounds stiff.

6/ Post before you feel ready

Publish now, watch the response, and make the next one better.

7/ Teach with stories

Pull in real examples and case studies that show your method working.

8/ Let your niche grow with you

Start narrow, then widen once people know what you are good at.

9/ Choose clear words

Stick to words people already know so every point is easy to repeat.

10/ Give before you ask

Build one lead magnet that solves a narrow, painful problem and give it away for an email.

You CAN use Claude to write content in your voice (instead of slop).
This is the exact system I use:

Most people assume that if you let AI write, you get slop.

And they're right…if you just open the chat box and start typing prompts.
But you can set Claude up to write like YOU. And if you do it right, people can't tell the difference.

It just takes a bit of work upfront.

Here's how to do it:

Step 1: Turn on memory

Go into Claude’s settings and turn memory on. This way Claude can build and update its memory as your style evolves, rules change, and standards increase.

Step 2: Create a dedicated project

Set up one project just for your content. Mine is completely separate from anything else I do, so it stays focused on one job - writing like me.

Step 3: Add your raw materials

Upload call transcripts, YouTube video transcripts, and your best work.

Choose the ones where the tone, pacing, and examples feel closest to how you want to write now. Claude needs to see what “good” looks like before it can copy it.

Step 4: Have Claude build your voice file

Ask Claude to build one file - voice.md - from everything you uploaded.

It will summarize all the elements that will make the output sound like how you speak.

Mine has a whole section just for words I've banned myself from using, like quietly and leveraged 🤮.

Step 5: Read everything and push back

This is the most important part, and most people skip it. Never just accept what it gives you. Tell it exactly what's off.

I never say "make it better." I say something like "this line's too formal, I'd never say it like that."

Step 6: Update your project every month

Come back every few months. Add new posts, emails, and call transcripts. Cut the ones that don't sound like you anymore.

I do this every 4-6 weeks because my style today isn't my style from a year ago.

An afternoon of work, and you never sound like a robot again.

items.content:
Most personal brands are forgettable.
The memorable ones have 4 things figured out:

1/ Their niche
2/ Their profile
3/ Their content mix
4/ They actually talk to the people who show up

Start doing this and in 30 days, the right people will remember you.

Here is the exact plan:

1/ Fix your profile

- Use a high quality, close-up photo with a solid background.
- Write your headline: who you help + how you help + proof.
- Use bullets in your About section to be clear what you can offer your audience, then end with a call to action.
- Put your lead magnets, like templates or courses, in your Featured section.
- Direct your custom button to your main offer. This will show on EVERY post.

The goal: people should know within seconds why they should follow you.

2/ Find your niche

- Write down your skills, your experience and the results you can drive.
- Pick one type of person who would benefit from that knowledge.
- Choose one painful problem they need solved.
- Name the clear solution only you can offer them.
- Put it together: "I help [who] solve [problem] so they can [result]."
- Use that sentence as a north star in your content.

"Career advice" is easy to forget. "Helping mid-level professionals land more interviews" is memorable.

3/ Create your content mix

- Share news from your niche and explain why it matters.
- Write about a common problem and show a new perspective.
- Teach one useful lesson people can apply that day.
- Tell stories from your life that have a valuable takeaway.
- Share useful resources like how-to guides and carousels people will want to save.
- Answer the objections that stop people from buying.

Some posts help new people find you. Some give them a reason to trust you. And some convince them to buy from you. No post should do all 3.

4/ Build your network

- This takes about 60 minutes a day.
- Comment on 5–10 posts in your niche before your post goes live.
- Add a real thought, example or question to each one.
- Once your post is live, reply to every comment.
- Send a short, personal message to the people who regularly engage.
- Connect with creators at your level in your niche.

This is probably the most important piece - creating real connection with your audience is the fastest way to become memorable to them.

I've done this with every new hire at WM Media.

We're a remote team and we do most things through a screen. But there are 2 things that are much better in person:

We help iconic leaders of iconic companies. Leaders of companies that are defining their industries, and you really feel that when you meet them.

But it's much harder to get that through a screen. So Adelaide and I drove out into rural Colorado, to visit one of our clients' sites.

We walked the site and got a tour of their manufacturing facility. Then the CEO sat down with us and told the story firsthand: what the company is trying to do, and why our work matters to it.

Once you've stood in the building and met the people, the work has a face.

The second is training.

In our line of work - world-class exec storytelling - the craft is learned through reps. Working remotely, I might give feedback 1-2x a day.

When we're sitting next to each other, I can turn and give feedback 3 or 4 times an hour :).

That's so important in the early days!

The flexibility of remote is great, but nothing replaces being in the same room.

Everybody says "build a personal brand."
Nobody tells you where to actually start.

Most people do 1 of 2 things. They either post random thoughts and hope something sticks, or they never start at all.

Both get you to the same place…nowhere.

In reality, the whole thing comes down to 7 steps:

Step 1: Fix your profile

Your banner, photo, headline, About and Featured sections should tell one story. who you help, what you help them do, and where to go next.

If a stranger can't work that out in 5 seconds, they bounce.

Step 2: Pick your niche

One person, one problem. Fill in this line: "I help [who] do [what] so they can [outcome]."

Saywhat started because I was spending too much time on LinkedIn instead of my actual work. I solved my own problem first, then found the people who shared it.

Step 3: Build a topic bank

Keep a running list of the real problems your audience complains about, the outlier posts in your niche, and the stories only you can tell. That list alone is months of content.

Step 4: Adapt what already works

Find posts in your niche that performed 2x better than average. Then adapt the topic, format or design for your audience.

ADAPT is the important word here. Don't copy. Make it your own!

Step 5: Write posts people save

Lead with proof. Name the pain and make it sting a little. Then give people 1-3 things they can do tomorrow. Useful posts get saved… and saved posts get you remembered.

Step 6: Set your content mix

Every post has ONE job. Post to grow your audience most days, post to build trust twice a week, post to convert once a week.

Step 7: Turn attention into relationships

Reply to every comment in the first hour. DM the people who keep showing up. Comment on other people's posts like a human, not a lead-gen bot.

You don't need all 7 on day one. Start with your profile this week and work down the list.

In a few months, you'll have what most people never build: a brand that works while you sleep.

items.content:
Your prospects delete your emails
faster than you delete pizza flyers.

The flyer at least targets someone who orders pizza.
Your email targets a job title.

After years in sales, here is the most valuable thing I learned:

Every deal starts with two things.

1. The right keyword, placed as early as possible in your pitch or your email.
2. The right timing.

Let me explain why timing became an obsession for me.
Over the last five years I sold for Deel and for cyber startups.

Deel has several products, and each one matches a precise moment in a company's life cycle. A company opening an office abroad has a need that did not exist a month earlier. Catch that moment and the situation dictates the pitch.

Same in cybersecurity: a fresh fundraise means shipping faster, hiring in waves, and a growing surface to attack.

Knowing this changed nothing about how hard it was.
Catching these moments was fully manual, and honestly discouraging. On 200 cold calls, you land on a good timing once, if you are lucky. Same odds on 500 or 1,000 cold emails.

The technique was right and the job still felt like a lottery.

In 2026, hoping you arrived at the right moment is no longer a strategy you're allowed to have. The tools exist now.

That's what I use lemlist agents for. 

I pick the signals that matter for my business (a fundraise, an office opening, a hiring spree on a specific role) and they scan daily. 

When one fires, the lead lands in my campaign, and the signal tells me both things at once: which words to open with, and that today is the day to reach out.

Since I made the switch, my cold email open rate went from 18% to 61%. And the same shift happened on my cold calls, because opening with the right keyword at the right moment works on the phone even better than in writing.

But the numbers are not even the real change.

I do a third of the volume I used to, and I close more than I ever did, because I spend my weeks talking to people instead of trying to talk to people.

And there is a side effect nobody mentions: confidence. Sending 500 emails into the void and dialing 150 numbers a week where nothing is happening quietly destroys yours. Reaching out where something just happened means getting taken seriously on almost every touch, and that changes how you sell everything.

The volume was never my problem. Arriving after the signature was.

Top performers book 1 meeting a day.
This has always been my goal. 

I don't log off until that meeting is booked.

Now you'll say I must never log off then, lol. But no.

This is a system that took me 2 years to build.

The pipeline I needed was already buried in my own CRM.

Here's the routine I run every morning with Attio, and the prompts I use.


✦ Play 1: the calls I already had

My warmest meeting of the day is usually someone who already sat on a call with us and then went quiet.

So before touching any cold list, I open Ask Attio and type:

→ "Show me every person who had a meeting with our team, has no open deal, and no activity in the last 60 days."

Attio syncs my calendar and logs every meeting straight onto the record, so it hands me a clean list of people I owe a follow-up.

I reopen the thread, reference something specific from our last call, and ask for 15 minutes.

That follow-up move books more meetings for me than any cold sequence ever has.


✦ Play 2: the movers

This one prints meetings.

When someone who already bought from us lands at a new company, they show up with budget and a reason to bring us along.

Attio keeps enriching my contacts in the background, so when a past customer changes company, the move surfaces on the record instead of slipping by.

→ "Which of our closed-won contacts changed companies recently?"

That's a list of champions walking into fresh budgets.

One warm follow-up, one meeting.


✦ Play 3: the funded accounts

I don't only recycle old conversations. Some mornings I want a brand new logo.

Attio enriches company records with funding data, so I can filter accounts that fit our ICP and have real money behind them.

→ "Show me companies in my target market that have raised over $5M and that we've never contacted."

A funded account means the budget is already there. I just need a reason to be relevant right now.

I qualify two or three, then reach out with something tied to what they just raised for.

Try it yourself: https://lnkd.in/enqX6TSr

Nothing here is clever.

In 2026 you'd have to be a little crazy to spend your days updating Salesforce by hand.

I just talk to my CRM now, like I'd talk to an LLM.

items.content:
Your LinkedIn profile ranks your posts now.
Every section on your profile feeds into how your posts get distributed.

LinkedIn's algorithm indexes your headline at 5x the weight of any other field on your profile. 
Optimized headlines get 40% more profile views. 

That means your banner, headline, featured content and experience all feed into whether your posts get shown to 100 people or 10,000.

Here's how mine is set up:

1. Banner communicates what I do and whom I help in one line without any clutter or extra visuals getting in the way.

2. Headline uses 150+ of the 220 characters LinkedIn gives you. Every unused character is a keyword you're not ranking for.

3. Featured section gets updated monthly with posts, resources, and offers that reflect current positioning.

4. Experience shows impact with numbers like revenue, results, and scale. Recruiters spend 6 seconds scanning, and numbers are what they stop on.

A strong profile makes every post work harder.
